cases.abstract: ConvNeXt investigates whether hierarchical vision Transformers' recognition performance can be matched by modernizing convolutional design and training without attention. A modern training recipe raises ResNet-50 ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy from 76.1% to 78.8%, motivating an architectural comparison that keeps this recipe fixed. Sequential modifications separate spatial filtering from channel mixing: large depthwise kernels operate before channel expansion, allowing wider spatial coverage while concentrating dense computation in pointwise layers. The resulting convolutional hierarchy also simplifies activation and normalization patterns, without shifted-window attention or relative position biases. At 384 x 384 resolution, ConvNeXt-B trained on ImageNet-1K reaches 85.1% top-1 accuracy versus Swin-B's 84.5%, with 12.5% higher inference throughput on a V100 GPU. Scaling data and capacity remains productive: after ImageNet-22K pretraining and ImageNet-1K fine-tuning at this resolution, ConvNeXt-XL reaches 87.8%. COCO detection and instance segmentation and ADE20K semantic segmentation yield performance comparable to or better than the evaluated Swin counterparts. The results show that competitive performance across these recognition tasks does not require the specialized attention modules used by Swin.
cases.methods: To widen spatial coverage without applying a dense large kernel across every channel pair, ConvNeXt separates spatial filtering from channel mixing. Each residual block first applies a 7 x 7 depthwise convolution at the input channel width. Pointwise layers then expand the channels fourfold and project them back, placing the large spatial kernel before the wider, dense transformations. This ordering reduces the depthwise operation's channel count compared with filtering after expansion, while preserving a separate channel-mixing stage. One LayerNorm and one GELU remain within each block; separate stride-two convolutions handle downsampling, with normalization at resolution transitions to stabilize training. These choices are evaluated sequentially under a fixed 300-epoch AdamW recipe and roughly controlled FLOPs, with three-seed averages in the smaller regime. Holding training fixed distinguishes the architectural trajectory from the initial recipe gain, although sequential changes and unequal intermediate costs limit attribution to individual components.
cases.results: Modernization improves both accuracy and measured inference throughput in the ImageNet-1K comparison at 384 x 384 resolution: ConvNeXt-B reaches 85.1% top-1 accuracy and 95.7 images per second, versus Swin-B's 84.5% and 85.1 images per second on a V100 GPU. The result therefore goes beyond a favorable FLOP count. A separate downstream comparison tests whether competitiveness extends beyond classification. With ImageNet-22K pretraining and Cascade Mask R-CNN under a 3x schedule, ConvNeXt-B obtains 54.0 box AP and 46.9 mask AP on COCO, compared with Swin-B's 53.0 and 45.8. However, the architectural trajectory does not support indiscriminate adoption of Transformer conventions: replacing ReLU with GELU alone leaves accuracy unchanged, kernels beyond 7 x 7 provide no further gain, and separate downsampling initially causes divergence until normalization is added at resolution changes. These mixed outcomes support the evaluated combination of convolutional choices, rather than treating any borrowed component as independently responsible for the final improvement.
cases.notes: Revision retains the initial contribution and comparisons. The abstract connects depthwise filtering before channel expansion to the fixed-recipe modernization question (Sections 2.1, 2.3-2.5); Methods explains the operation without claiming isolated causality. Results links Table 1's V100 classification comparison to Table 3's separately pretrained COCO comparison, then qualifies component adoption using Sections 2.5-2.6. The 82.0% roadmap endpoint and 82.1% Table 1 entry remain distinct and are omitted. Scaling evidence retains ImageNet-22K pretraining and 384 x 384 fine-tuning. Multimodal and structured-output suitability remains untested.

cases.abstract: High-quality novel-view synthesis must reconcile reconstruction fidelity with the cost of interactive rendering. We represent static scenes as anisotropic 3D Gaussians initialized from sparse structure-from-motion points, optimizing their geometry, opacity, and spherical-harmonic appearance. Cloning small Gaussians and splitting large ones adapt the representation to missing detail, while pruning removes ineffective primitives. Projecting these Gaussians into splats enables a differentiable tile-based rasterizer to share depth sorting across pixels; its backward pass updates all contributing splats without a fixed count limit. Evaluation on 13 real scenes and bounded synthetic scenes tests both quality and rendering speed. After 30,000 iterations, real-scene dataset averages reach 134-154 frames per second on an A6000 GPU at their respective native resolutions, with approximately 27-42 minutes of training. Quality improves over InstantNGP and Plenoxels and is competitive with Mip-NeRF360, although Mip-NeRF360 retains higher PSNR on its own dataset. Interactive rendering therefore accompanies competitive reconstruction rather than uniform metric superiority; stored models are substantially larger than neural radiance-field baselines, and poor view coverage or changes in blending order can still produce artifacts.
cases.methods: A differentiable renderer must preserve gradients through many overlapping splats without allocating an arbitrarily long list for each pixel. The rasterizer divides the screen into 16 x 16 tiles, duplicates projected Gaussians for overlapping tiles, and performs one GPU radix sort keyed by tile identifier and depth. Each tile loads batches into shared memory and blends splats front to back until a pixel's opacity saturates. Sharing this order avoids per-pixel sorting, but makes blending approximate when splats are large. The backward pass reuses the sorted tile lists in reverse, recovering intermediate blending quantities from the final accumulated opacity rather than storing each step. Consequently, storage per pixel need not grow with the number of contributing splats, and gradient computation has no predetermined splat-count cap. This connects rendering speed with an optimization requirement: reducing visibility-processing overhead while retaining updates through variable scene depth complexity.
cases.results: On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, the 30,000-iteration Gaussian model improves SSIM to 0.815 from the published reference's 0.792 and lowers LPIPS to 0.214 from 0.237, yet PSNR falls short at 27.21 versus 27.69 dB. Thus, competitive reconstruction is metric-dependent. Longer optimization also changes the deployment tradeoff: increasing the budget from 7,000 to 30,000 iterations raises PSNR from 25.60 to 27.21 dB, while average A6000 training time rises from 6 minutes 25 seconds to 41 minutes 33 seconds and rendering falls from 160 to 134 frames per second. Stored parameters grow from 523 to 734 MB, far above Mip-NeRF360's 8.6 MB. Preserving gradients is consequential, not merely an implementation detail: on Truck, capping updates at ten front-most splats lowers 30,000-iteration PSNR from 24.81 to 13.84 dB and destabilizes optimization. The tested renderer therefore supports interactive viewing with substantial storage costs; its fast visibility approximation can still produce popping when large splats change blending order.
cases.notes: The abstract retains representation adaptation, uncapped gradients, and the speed-quality tradeoff. Methods explains how shared sorting and reverse traversal avoid per-pixel histories (Section 6); Results tests quality and storage promises with Table 1, then connects the gradient-cap failure to this design (Table 3). Real-scene rates and times are dataset averages at differing native resolutions. Mip-NeRF360 quality on its dataset is published, not rerun; its four-A100, 12-hour training cost is not treated as a matched A6000 comparison. Storage figures are optimized parameters, not peak GPU allocation. Synthetic random-initialization success does not negate its adverse real-scene ablation.
